en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.1 (SN 27.1, PTS SN iii 232) 1. The Chapter on Defilements: The Discourse on the Eye “Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering. Whatever is suffering is non-self. Whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “The ear is impermanent… The nose is impermanent… The tongue is impermanent… The body is impermanent… The mind is impermanent. Whatever is impermanent is suffering. Whatever is suffering is non-self. Whatever is non-self should be seen with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. “Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for the eye, that is a defilement of the mind.
Whatever desire and lust there is for the ear, that is a defilement of the mind."
Whatever desire and lust there is for the nose, this is a defilement of the mind.
Whatever desire and lust there is for the tongue, this is a defilement of the mind.
Whatever desire and lust there is for the body, this is a defilement of the mind.
“Whatever desire and lust there is for the mind, that is a defilement of the mind.
But when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned these mental defilements in these six instances, his mind inclines toward renunciation.
A mind cultivated by renunciation appears wieldy with respect to those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.”
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.2 (SN 27.2, PTS SN iii 232) 1.
The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga)
The Discourse on Form. At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for forms, that is a corruption of the mind."
He who [clings] to sounds … he who [clings] to odors … he who [clings] to tastes …
Whatever desire and lust there is for tactile objects...
whatever desire and lust there is for mental phenomena—this is a defilement of the mind.
But when, monks, a bhikkhu has abandoned this mental defilement in these six instances, his mind inclines toward renunciation.
“A mind cultivated by renunciation appears wieldy regarding those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Thus was the second [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 27.3 (SN 27.3, PTS SN iii 232).
1. The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga), the Discourse on Consciousness (Viññāṇasutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for eye-consciousness, that is a defilement of the mind.
Whatever [desire and lust] there is for ear-consciousness… whatever [desire and lust] there is for nose-consciousness…”

Whatever desire and lust there is in tongue-consciousness … whatever desire and lust there is in body-consciousness … whatever desire and lust there is in mind-consciousness, this is a corruption of the mind.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned the mental defilement in these six instances, his mind inclines toward renunciation.
A mind cultivated by renunciation appears wieldy with respect to those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Thus [ends] the third.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 27.4 (SN 27.4, PTS SN iii 233) 1. Kilesavagga Samphassasutta “Bhikkhus, when there is contact, there is feeling; when there is no contact, there is no feeling. When there is contact, there is perception; when there is no contact, there is no perception. When there is contact, there is volitional formations; when there is no contact, there are no volitional formations. When there is contact, there is consciousness; when there is no contact, there is no consciousness. When there is feeling, there is craving; when there is no feeling, there is no craving. When there is feeling, there is perception; when there is no feeling, there is no perception. When there is feeling, there is volitional formations; when there is no feeling, there are no volitional formations. When there is feeling, there is consciousness; when there is no feeling, there is no consciousness. When there is perception, there is craving; when there is no perception, there is no craving. When there is perception, there is feeling; when there is no perception, there is no feeling. When there is perception, there is volitional formations; when there is no perception, there are no volitional formations. When there is perception, there is consciousness; when there is no perception, there is no consciousness. When there are volitional formations, there is craving; when there are no volitional formations, there is no craving. When there are volitional formations, there is feeling; when there are no volitional formations, there is no feeling. When there are volitional formations, there is perception; when there are no volitional formations, there is no perception. When there are volitional formations, there is consciousness; when there are no volitional formations, there is no consciousness. When there is consciousness, there is craving; when there is no consciousness, there is no craving. When there is consciousness, there is feeling; when there is no consciousness, there is no feeling. When there is consciousness, there is perception; when there is no consciousness, there is no perception. When there is consciousness, there are volitional formations; when there is no consciousness, there are no volitional formations.”
At Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for eye-contact—that is an affliction of the mind.
Whatever [desire and lust there is] for ear-contact..."
Whatever [feeling] arises in nose-contact … whatever [feeling] arises in tongue-contact … whatever [feeling] arises in body-contact …
Whatever desire and lust there is for mind-contact, this is a defilement of the mind.
But when, monks, for a monk...
[and so on] ...regarding those things to be realized through direct knowledge.”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 27.5 (SN 27.5, PTS SN iii 233) 1.
The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga)
The Discourse on What is Born of Contact. Setting: Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for feeling born of eye-contact—that is a corruption of the mind.”
Whatever [craving] there is for feeling born of ear-contact … whatever [craving] there is for feeling born of nose-contact … whatever [craving] there is for feeling born of tongue-contact …

Whatever desire and lust there is for feeling born of body-contact … for feeling born of mind-contact, this is a defilement of the mind. When, monks, for a bhikkhu … [as before] … [he knows, "There is desire and lust for feeling born of mind-contact; this is a defilement of the mind"].
“...regarding those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
The fifth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 27.6 (SN 27.6, PTS SN iii 233).
1. The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga).
Discourse on Perceptions (Saññāsutta). Setting at Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for the perception of forms, that is a defilement of the mind. Whatever [desire and lust there is] for the perception of sounds … whatever [desire and lust there is] for the perception of odors …”
Whatever desire and lust there is for the perception of tastes … for the perception of tangibles … for the perception of mental phenomena, this is a defilement of the mind.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu ... [as before] ...
has direct knowledge regarding those things that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
The sixth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.7 (SN 27.7, PTS SN iii 233) 1. Kilesavagga Sañcetanāsutta (The Discourse on Volition) “Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of volitional formations. What three? Volitional formations of the body, volitional formations of speech, and volitional formations of the mind. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of volitional formations.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for volition regarding forms, that is a corruption of the mind.
Whatever [desire and lust there is] for volition regarding sounds …”
Whatever [volition] through volition regarding odors...
whatever [volition] through volition regarding tastes...
whatever [volition] through volition regarding tangibles...
“Whatever desire and lust there is for volition regarding mental phenomena, this is a defilement of the mind.
But when, monks, a monk... [as before] ...regarding those things to be realized through direct knowledge.”
Seventh.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 27.8 (SN 27.8, PTS SN iii 234) 1.
The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga)
The Discourse on Craving.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
"Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for craving for forms—that is an affliction of the mind."
Whatever [craving] for the craving for tastes… whatever [craving] for the craving for odors… whatever [craving] for the craving for flavors…
Whatever desire and lust there is for craving for tangible objects … whatever desire and lust there is for craving for mental phenomena, this is a defilement of the mind. But when,
monks, for a monk … [as before] … [the mind is purified].
“...in the states to be realized through direct knowledge.
Thus [ends] the eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 27.9 (SN 27.9, PTS SN iii 234).
1. The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga). The Discourse on Elements (Dhātusutta).
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for the earth element— that is a defilement of the mind. Whatever [desire and lust there is] for the water element… whatever [desire and lust there is] for the fire element…”
Whatever desire and lust there is for the air element … for the space element … for the consciousness element, that is a defilement of the mind.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has abandoned mental defilement in these six instances, his mind inclines toward renunciation.
A mind cultivated by renunciation appears wieldy regarding those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 27.10 (SN 27.10, PTS SN iii 234) 1. The Chapter on Defilements (Kilesavagga) The Discourse on the Aggregates (Khandhasutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates subject to clinging.”
At Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, whatever desire and lust there is for form, that is a corruption of the mind... whatever desire and lust there is for consciousness, that is a corruption of the mind.
But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned this mental corruption in these five instances, his mind inclines toward renunciation.”
“A mind cultivated by renunciation appears wieldy regarding those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Tenth. The First Chapter on Defilements.
Its summary verse:
Eye, form, and consciousness,
contact, and feeling.
Perception, volition, and craving—
these ten, by way of the aggregates,
constitute the Section on Defilements. This concludes [the section].
